sections.normalized_html:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] be the number of damaged packs in a randomly selected box.

First, we write down the null and alternative hypotheses:

  • [MATH: H_0\mathbin{:}\: X\sim B(3,p)]

  • [MATH: H_1\mathbin{:}\:X\not\sim B(3,p)]

The number of observations is

[MATH: N=20+30+8+2 = 60.]

We can calculate an estimate of [MATH: p,] which we denote as [MATH: \hat p,] as follows:

[MATH: p^(^)|= (total number of successes)/(total number of trials); = (∑(x_{i} ⋅ O_{i}))/(n ⋅ N),] where [MATH: O_i] is the observed frequency for the [MATH: i]th observation, [MATH: N] is the number of observations, and [MATH: n] is the number of trials in each Binomial sequence. So, in our case, we have

[MATH: p^(^)|= (0 ⋅ 20 + 1 ⋅ 30 + 2 ⋅ 8 + 3 ⋅ 2)/(3 ⋅ (60)); ≈ 0.2889] rounded to four decimal places.

Therefore, the proposed distribution is [MATH: X\sim B(3,0.2889).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to conduct chi-square goodness-of-fit tests to determine whether some sample data fit a binomial distribution.

Content:
First, let's remind ourselves of some basic facts.

Content:
- Given a random variable [MATH: X\sim B(n, p),] the probability mass function of [MATH: X] is given by
[MATH: P(X = x)|= ((n)/(x))p^{x}(1 − p)^{n − x}.]
- Given a random sample of size [MATH: N] drawn from [MATH: X\sim B(n,p),] the expected frequency of the outcome [MATH: X=x] is given by
[MATH: E_x = N\cdot P(X=x) .]

Content:
Let's get some practice at computing expected values using the binomial distribution.

---

- [MATH: H_1\mathbin{:}\:X\not\sim B(3, 0.4)]

| [MATH: x_i] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] |

Under the null hypothesis, we have that [MATH: X\sim B(3, 0.4).] Therefore,

Let's calculate the probability of each value of [MATH: X{:}]
[MATH: P(X = 0)|= ((3)/(0))(0.4)^{0}(0.6)^{3} = 0.216; P(X = 1)|= ((3)/(1))(0.4)^{1}(0.6)^{2} = 0.432; P(X = 2)|= ((3)/(2))(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{1} = 0.288; P(X = 3)|= ((3)/(3))(0.4)^{3}(0.6)^{0} = 0.064]
